clinicalPearls: Polydactyly is duplication of a digit and is classified by location: preaxial (thumb or radial side), central (index to ring), and postaxial (little finger or ulnar side)
Postaxial polydactyly is common, frequently familial (autosomal dominant), and more prevalent in children of African ancestry; it may be isolated or syndromic
Preaxial (thumb) duplication is graded by the Wassel-Flatt classification according to the most proximal level of skeletal duplication, from a bifid distal phalanx to a duplicated metacarpal
Central polydactyly is less common, is often hidden within a syndactyly (polysyndactyly), and involves complex bony and tendinous connections that are difficult to reconstruct

Syndromic associations must be considered: preaxial forms with conditions such as Holt-Oram syndrome and Fanconi anaemia, and postaxial forms with Ellis-van Creveld, Bardet-Biedl, Meckel-Gruber, and trisomy 13
A well-formed extra digit is not simply excised; reconstruction preserves the most functional bone, joint, ligaments, tendons, and nail, and reconstructs collateral ligament stability
Surgery is timed to optimise function and appearance, generally in early childhood
reference.pathophysiology: Polydactyly arises from disordered patterning of the developing limb bud along the anteroposterior (radioulnar) axis. Abnormal signalling, notably of the sonic hedgehog pathway acting through the zone of polarising activity, produces one or more supernumerary digits. The duplicated ray may be a rudimentary soft-tissue tag or a fully formed digit with its own bones, joints, and tendons. Depending on which part of the axis is affected, the extra digit lies on the radial (preaxial), central, or ulnar (postaxial) side of the hand, and disturbances of these same signalling pathways underlie the many syndromic forms.
additionalDifferentials: Syndactyly or polysyndactyly, which may coexist
Macrodactyly (an enlarged rather than duplicated digit)
Constriction ring sequence with accessory tissue
additionalInvestigations: Radiographs of the hand to define the level of skeletal duplication (for example Wassel-Flatt grading of the thumb)
Family history and examination of relatives, as postaxial forms are often autosomal dominant
Clinical screening for syndromic features affecting the heart, kidneys, retina, and growth
Echocardiography where a heart-hand or VACTERL association is suspected
Genetic evaluation when the pattern is syndromic, central, or bilateral
redFlags: Features suggesting a serious syndrome, such as a cardiac anomaly, renal disease, retinal dystrophy, or marrow-failure risk
Central polydactyly or polysyndactyly with complex functional impairment
A duplicated thumb that is unstable or deviating, threatening pinch function
reference.prognosis: Isolated postaxial and most preaxial duplications have an excellent outcome after well-planned reconstruction; residual problems can include joint instability, angular deviation, stiffness, and a reconstructed thumb that is smaller than normal, while central forms are more prone to stiffness and imperfect appearance.
pitfalls: Simply tying off or amputating a duplicated digit without reconstructing the collateral ligaments, leaving instability or deviation
Discarding the more functional of two duplicated thumbs
Failing to look for syndromic associations
Underestimating the complexity of central polysyndactyly
management: Excision of a rudimentary pedunculated postaxial digit, by suture ligation or formal removal of the soft-tissue remnant
Reconstructive surgery for a well-formed duplicated digit that preserves the most functional bone, joint, tendons and nail and restores collateral ligament stability rather than simple amputation
Timing and technique of thumb (preaxial) reconstruction guided by the Wassel-Flatt level of skeletal duplication, undertaken by a specialist paediatric hand surgeon
Complex staged reconstruction for central polysyndactyly given the intricate bony and tendinous interconnections
Screening for syndromic associations affecting the heart, kidneys, retina and growth, with echocardiography where a heart-hand or VACTERL association is suspected
Postoperative hand therapy and monitoring for residual joint instability, angular deviation and stiffness
Genetic counselling and examination of relatives given autosomal dominant inheritance of many postaxial forms, with genetic evaluation for syndromic, central or bilateral patterns
